item.title: [NH] NH Education Daily — Hot Off the Press: The Ballot Decisions That Will Reshape NH School Districts
item.description:
A one-hour breaking special, October 13, 2026: Three weeks before November 3, every NH voter faces Question 2 — the HB 1300 school tax cap. Alex and Jordan unpack what the ballot says vs. what RSA 32:5-i actually does, Londonderry's warning of million in cuts, district-by-district impacts from Hudson to Oyster River to Mascenic, the failed court challenges, and what real voters are posting on social media right now — verified posts from both sides. Plus: what a levy cap means for special education's unfunded mandates.

item.title: [NH] NH Education Deep Dive — Who's Teaching Special Ed? NH's Staffing Shortage
item.description:
The NH Fiscal Policy Institute's new report projects 1,114 teacher openings a year through 2034, with staffing down 5.7%, the pipeline halved, and teachers earning a third less than comparable professionals. Alex and Jordan unpack what it means for special education — endorsement barriers, the para crisis, the contracting trap, FAPE risk — and what districts can actually do about it.

item.title: [NH] NH Education Deep Dive — The Burden Shift: How HB 581 Rewrote the Rules of Special Ed Disputes in New Hampshire
item.description:
In 2021, New Hampshire moved the burden of proof in special education due process hearings off of parents and onto school districts. Alex and Jordan break down HB 581 — what changed, what it means for parents and districts, and what it demands of NH special education teams in their daily work. Educational guidance, not legal advice.
Work with our consultant One-on-one help for parents from an NH special education administrator: IEP reviews, meeting prep, Prior Written Notice — what to ask for, and how to ask for it. Consults $250 — book a consult: [link]
Sources - HB 581 as introduced (2021), full bill text (PDF), NH General Court archives: https://gencourt.state.nh.us/BillHistory/SofS_Archives/2021/house/HB581H.pdf - RSA 186-C:16-b, current text — Due Process Hearing; Appeal (see paragraph III-a), official NH General Court statute site: https://www.GenCourt.state.nh.us/rsa/html/XV/186-C/186-C-mrg.htm - "NH Changes Law Regarding Burden of Proof in Special Education Due Process Hearings," Disability Rights Center–New Hampshire, Aug 2, 2021: https://drcnh.org/statements/burden-of-proof-in-due-process-hearings/ - "Sununu signs bill shifting burden of proof in special education hearings to schools," Keene Sentinel (via NH Bulletin), 2021: https://www.keenesentinel.com/news/local/sununu-signs-bill-shifting-burden-of-proof-in-special-education-hearings-to-schools/article_78864d50-12bb-5eac-8d49-78cb31042cbf.html - NH Department of Education, FY26 "Rules and Laws in Excess" chart (PDF): http://doe.nhdoit.acsitefactory.com/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/sonh/fy26-nh-rules-and-laws-in-excess-chart.pdf - 2025 Compilation of Education Legislation, NH School Boards Association (PDF) — includes HB 754 (automatic discovery): https://nhsba.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/2025-Compilation-of-Ed-Legislation-for-2025-Legislative-Summary.pdf - "New Hampshire Shifted the Due Process Burden to Schools in IEP Disputes. item.title: [New Hampshire] Deep Dive — State Complaints, ESY, and Compensatory Education
item.description:
This deep dive walks through the three dispute tools that meet in one file folder: the state complaint under 34 CFR 300.151 through 300.153 and New Hampshire's Ed 1121 process (who can file, the sixty-day clock, the commissioner's signed decision, the twenty-day reconsideration rule, and the public complaint summaries required by RSA 186-C:5-a); extended school year under 34 CFR 300.106 and New Hampshire's Ed 1110.01 (individual team determination, the regression and recoupment standard, and the factors beyond regression); and compensatory education under the qualitative "but for" standard of Reid v. District of Columbia, 401 F.3d 516 (D.C. Cir. 2005), including the First Circuit's Pihl decision and real New Hampshire complaint orders that required districts to deliver compensatory services. The episode closes with the documentation habits that decide these cases in practice. Plain-English explanations of the governing rules, with settled law distinguished from practical interpretation, for working New Hampshire special education teachers and case managers.
### Sources
- 34 CFR 300.151–300.153 (state complaint procedures, remedies, and filing contents): https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/34/300.152 — also search eCFR at ecfr.gov for "300.151 adoption of State complaint procedures" and "300.153 complaint contents" to read the adopted text of all three sections side by side. - New Hampshire Rules for the Education of Children with Disabilities, Ed 1121 (complaint process) and Ed 1110.01 (extended school year): full rule text at https://www.gc.nh.gov/rules/state_agencies/ed1100.html — find Ed 1121 in Part Ed 1121 and Ed 1110.01 in Part Ed 1110 on that page; annotated copy with cross-references in the Guide to the NH Standards for the Education of Children with Disabilities at https://picnh.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Guide-to-the-NH-Standards-3.1.2024.pdf - NH Department of Education, Special Education State Complaint Process flow chart (sufficiency triage, investigation, commissioner's decision, corrective action): http://doe.nhdoit.acsitefactory.com/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/sonh/flow-chart-special-education-complaint-process.pdf - NH Special Education Procedural Safeguards Handbook (complaint steps, sixty-day decision, twenty-day reconsideration, corrective action during reconsideration): https://core-docs.s3.amazonaws.com/documents/asset/uploaded_file/163/District/2787706/NH_Special_Education_Procedural_Safeguards_Handbook.pdf - RSA 186-C:5-a (state complaint tracking system and required public posting of redacted complaint summaries): https://law.justia.com/codes/new-hampshire/title-xv/chapter-186-c/section-186-c-5-a/ - NH Department of Education, Special Education State Complaint #25-35 (corrective action plan ordering the team to determine missed progress and implement compensatory services): http://doe.nhdoit.acsitefactory.com/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/sonh/case-25-35.pdf - NH Department of Education, Special Education Complaint 22-04 (late-start speech and language services during the extended school year period): http://doe.nhdoit.acsitefactory.com/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/sonh/case-22-04.pdf - Reid ex rel. Reid v. District of Columbia, 401 F.3d 516 (D.C. Cir. 2005) (qualitative compensatory education standard): https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/401/516/551622/ - Pihl v. Massachusetts Department of Education, 9 F.3d 184 (1st Cir. 1993) (compensatory education available after eligibility ends): https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/9/184/540521/ - OSEP, "Return to School Roadmap: Development and Implementation of Individualized Education Programs in the Least Restrictive Environment under the IDEA" (Sept. 30, 2021), Question E-2 (a child may receive both ESY and compensatory services): https://sites.ed.gov/idea/idea-files/return-to-school-roadmap-development-and-implementation-of-ieps/ - 34 CFR 300.106 (extended school year services): search eCFR at ecfr.gov for "300.106 extended school year services" to read the full regulation text, including the prohibitions on limiting ESY by disability category or by type, amount, or duration. - Disability Rights Center–NH, "Filing a Special Education Complaint" (plain-language walkthrough of the NH investigation and decision process): https://drcnh.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/SPED_File_Complaint.pdf

item.title: The Plan Nobody Audits: Section 504's Quiet Quadrupling
item.description:
This deep dive examines the fastest-growing accommodation system in American public schools: plans under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 held by students who do not have IEPs. Drawing on the U.S. Department of Education's Civil Rights Data Collection for 2023–24 and the leading published research, Alex and Jordan walk through what a Section 504 plan is and how its three-part eligibility test differs from the IDEA; how the "504-only" rate climbed from 1.1% of students in 2009–10 to 3.9% in 2021–22 and about 1.9 million students (4%) in 2023–24; why rates range from near double the national average in Texas and New Hampshire to below half in New Mexico and Mississippi, with individual Texas middle schools above 30% and other schools at zero; the documented skew toward White students (60% of 504-only students against 44% of enrollment) and, in the first study to link school records to IRS tax data, toward higher-income families (2.9% vs. 1.5%), even as IEPs run the opposite way; the measured response of 504 enrollment to the College Board's 2017 decision to honor school accommodations on the SAT automatically; the costs of both over-identification and under-identification; and the central evidentiary gap — no national breakdown of 504 plans by condition and no national audit of 504 eligibility has ever been published, so claims about how many plans are "unnecessary" exceed what the evidence can support. Plain-English explanations, with every number sourced and the limits of the evidence stated on air.
### Sources
- U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights, "A First Look: The Civil Rights Data Collection, 2023–24" (September 2026) — 19% of students with disabilities (15% IDEA; 4% / ~1.9M Section 504 only); White students 60% of 504-only vs. 44% of enrollment; boys 56% of 504-only: https://www.ed.gov/media/document/2023-24-first-look-civil-rights-data-collection-september-30-2026-114593.pdf - Perry A. Zirkel, "Concerns About Misidentification of '504-Only' Students," ATPE News, March 30, 2026 — 1.1% (2009–10) to 3.9% (2021–22); Texas 7.6%; 23 of the top 25 districts (14.4%–17.4%); Texas middle schools at 23.1%–30.1%; three-part eligibility test; no federal/state funding; costs of over- and under-identification; Texas dyslexia analysis: https://atpenews.org/concerns-about-misidentification-of-504-only-students/ - Perry A. Zirkel, "Mis-identifying '504-Only' Students," eSchool News, February 6, 2026 — New Hampshire and Texas at almost double the national rate; New Mexico and Mississippi at less than half; California 2.1% with districts ranging 0%–13.9% and schools 0%–24.2%: https://www.eschoolnews.com/innovative-teaching/2026/02/06/mis-identifying-504-only-students/ - Zirkel et al., analysis of the 2009–10 Civil Rights Data Collection, Journal of Disability Policy Studies (2014), reported by Education Week — 504-only rates: White 1.26%, Black 0.57%, Hispanic 0.50%; Title I schools 0.84% vs. non-Title I 1.23%: https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/students-with-504-plans-more-likely-to-be-white-enrolled-in-non-title-i-schools/2014/08 - Holler & Zirkel, national survey of Section 504-only students (2008), reported by Education Week — mid-2000s rate of about 1.2%; ADHD the most commonly listed impairment, diabetes next: https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/counting-section-504-students/2008/03 - Ainsworth et al., Oregon study linking school records (2008–09 to 2018–19) to IRS tax data (paper released January 2026), and Tiffany Liu, study of 504 enrollment after the College Board's 2017 SAT accommodation policy (March 2026), both reported by The 74 / Disability Scoop, June 9, 2026 — 504 receipt 2.9% near the top of the income distribution vs. 1.5% near the bottom; IEP receipt about 25% among the most disadvantaged; verbatim comments from Nick Ainsworth, Paul Morgan, Ben Lovett, Miriam Nunberg, and Christopher Cleveland: https://www.disabilityscoop.com/2026/06/09/wealthy-students-more-likely-to-get-disability-accommodations-study-finds/32038/ - Tiffany Liu's College Board finding as also reported by Education Daly — the 504 enrollment response about 24% larger in the most affluent communities than in high-poverty schools: https://www.educationdaly.us/p/we-need-to-talk-about-504-plans - U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights, "Dear Colleague Letter and Resource Guide on Students with ADHD" (July 26, 2016) — districts must not assume that strong academic performance rules out a substantial limitation in a major life activity: https://www.wrightslaw.com/law/memos/ocr/sec504.adhd.2016.pdf - Disability Scoop, "Nearly 1 In 5 Public School Students Have IEPs Or 504 Plans" (October 19, 2026) — the 19% total is up from 17% in the prior (2021–22) collection: https://www.disabilityscoop.com/2026/10/19/nearly-1-in-5-public-school-students-have-ieps-or-504-plans/32226/

item.title: The List Nobody Can See: Inside the Child Care Food Program's Seven-Year Blacklist
item.description:
One routine Federal Register notice this fall renewed the paperwork behind the National Disqualified List — the Child and Adult Care Food Program's national bar on institutions, sponsoring organizations, day care home providers, and the individuals who run them. This deep dive opens up the machine: how a review finding becomes a "serious deficiency," how the corrective-action clock runs, why quitting does not save you, the appeal you get — and the six decisions 7 CFR 226.6(k)(3) says you can never appeal — and how a listing lasts seven years, or longer if a program debt is unpaid. Plus the vagueness problem the National CACFP Association put in writing (the same citation can mean a serious management problem in one state or "three small errors on a reimbursement claims form" in another), the patchwork early-removal door, the Feeding Our Future record that explains why the list exists, and the 2024 proposed rule (FNS-2024-0005) that would rebuild the process — still unfinalized. USDA does not publish the list or its size; where the public record runs out, this episode says so.
Sources: - 7 CFR 226.6 (CACFP State agency responsibilities — serious deficiency process at (c), National Disqualified List at (c)(7), administrative review at (k), day care home reviews at (l)): https://www.casemine.com/regulation/us/640f05fa8b0a3c5be33657ac/amp (also available at eCFR, Title 7, Part 226, §226.6) - USDA Food and Nutrition Service, "Proposed Rule: Serious Deficiency Process in the CACFP and SFSP" (docket FNS-2024-0005; comments due May 21, 2024; page updated February 4, 2026): https://fns-prod.azureedge.us/cn/fr-022124 - Proposed rule as published, 89 FR 13150 (February 21, 2024): https://www.cacfp.org/assets/pdf/SD+Propsoed+Rule+FR+Document+2024-02108/ - National CACFP Association (National CACFP Sponsors Association), comment letter on FNS-2024-0005, May 17, 2024 (signed Lisa Mack, President & CEO): https://files.constantcontact.com/e5582ed6201/f25b5196-65c4-4976-9cad-8cd96d1c625c.pdf - National CACFP Association, "NCA Response – National Disqualified List Information Collection," August 5, 2026: https://www.cacfp.org/2026/08/05/nca-response-national-disqualified-list-information-collection/ - National CACFP Association, Quarterly Policy Update, October 2026 (NDL information-collection comment summary): https://www.cacfp.org/2026/10/07/quarterly-policy-update-october-2026/ - USDA Food and Nutrition Service, "Why CACFP Is Important" (program scale and authority): https://fns-prod.azureedge.us/cacfp/why-cacfp-important - item.description:

item.title: [Maine] Education Trends — Chronic Absenteeism: One in Four Students, and the Long Climb Back
item.description:
One in four Maine students is chronically absent — the rate fell from a 31.1 percent pandemic peak to about 24 percent and then stalled — and this hour examines who is missing school, why, what five million lost instructional hours cost, and the Maine responses with results behind them, from the Maine Engagement and Attendance Center and early warning systems to Maine Indian Education's drop from the fifties to 19.6 percent.
Sources: Maine Department of Education, Data Warehouse — Chronic Absenteeism (definition: enrolled at least 10 days, missed 10% or more of days enrolled, excused or unexcused) and Enrollment: https://www.maine.gov/doe/data-reporting/reporting/warehouse/visualizations Maine Department of Education, Maine's Model of School Support (chronic absenteeism as an accountability indicator): https://www.maine.gov/doe/Testing_Accountability/model Maine Engagement and Attendance Center (MEAC, established 2024; national Attendance Works figures cited there: 28% national rate in 2022-23, 30% peak, 16% in 2018-19; Maine 31% in 2021-22, 27% in 2022-23, 24% in 2023-24): https://www11.maine.gov/doe/index.php/meac Maine KIDS COUNT Data Center, Chronic Absenteeism (24.4% in 2024-25; 40,980 students; economically disadvantaged 34.5% vs 15.7% for higher-income students): https://datacenter.aecf.org/data/tables/10836-chronic-absenteeism?loc=21&loct=2 Maine Education Association, How Count ME In! is Tackling Chronic Absenteeism Across Maine (24.1% / nearly 41,000 students in 2023-24; peak 31.1% / 53,265 in 2021-22; 16.5% in 2017-18; 5,000,000 instructional hours lost in 2023-24; Jess Anderson quote; teacher-call timing at 1-3 and 4-6 days): https://maineea.org/maineeducatoronline/how-count-me-in-is-tackling-chronic-absenteeism-across-maine/ Count ME In!, For Families (barriers: transportation, work schedules, caregiving, housing, long distances, weather, rural access; support-focused documentation steps): https://www.countmeinmaine.org/for-families Maine DOE Newsroom, Maine Engagement and Attendance Center Continues Bringing Statewide Partners Together (June 17 meeting; MEAC partners Count ME In! and Maine PBIS; proactive root-cause mission): https://mainedoenews.net/2026/09/04/maine-engagement-and-attendance-center-continues-bringing-statewide-partners-together-to-strengthen-student-attendance/ Bureau of Indian Education, Maine Indian Education Posts Landmark Gains in Attendance and Achievement (systemwide 19.6% in 2024-25; Indian Island School 13.1%; Sipayik Elementary 18.7%; Indian Township School 27.0%; Maine statewide ~24%): https://www.bie.edu/news-article/maine-indian-education-posts-landmark-gains-attendance-and-achievement-superintendent Maine Department of Education, BARR 2026 State Handout (92 BARR schools, 11,250 students, 2,667 educators, vs 463 non-BARR schools; chronic absenteeism decline 14.6 points in BARR schools): https://www.maine.gov/doe/sites/maine.gov.doe/files/inline-files/BARR%20-%202026%20State%20Hadnout%20-%207.22.2026.pdf University of Southern Maine, Maine Education Policy Research Institute, 2026 report for policymakers (enrollment roughly 4% below pre-pandemic; chronic absenteeism 31% in 2021-22, 24% in 2023-24, 16% pre-pandemic): https://usm.maine.edu/cepare/wp-content/uploads/sites/481/2026/07/2026_June_MEPRI-Report_Implications-for-Policymakers_FINAL.pdf Brewer School Department, Chronic Absenteeism and Attendance Information (Maine compulsory attendance ages 7-17; absent if not present for more than 50% of the day; state reporting and truancy reporting to DHHS and law enforcement): https://www.breweredu.org/article/70421
Verification steps for items without a stable URL: For the Maine Engagement and Attendance Center Attendance Tracker results (28% average decline in chronically absent students and 32% decline in students failing one or more courses after two years), search maine.gov for "Maine Engagement and Attendance Center Year in Review" and open the Student Supports MEAC Year-in-Review PDF dated June 3, 2026. For the Portland Public Schools high school chronic absenteeism figure of about 42 percent, search the Citizen Portal Portland Public Schools (Maine) feed for the school board meeting summary dated September 22, 2026. For the rural school-based health centers study, search PubMed Central for "School-Based Health Centers and School Attendance in Rural Areas."
